song.title: Caterpillar Munch
song.author: Mark and Helen Johnson
song.summary: A song for younger voices, this follows the caterpillar as he fattens himself up on his journey to butterfly freedom. The vocal arrangement on the recording mirrors his growth from one verse to the next – from duet, to group, to ensemble.
song.teachingTips:
• Warm up the facial muscles ready to sing using exaggerated ‘chewing’ and ‘munching’ actions.
  • Notice how the melody moves mainly by leaps, but then descends by steps (a scale) in bars 7 and 11. Indicating these intervals in the air with your hand fl at in front of you will help your singers to pitch the intervals correctly.
  • Try getting the children to raise their eyebrows (or caterpillars!) to help get their voices up to the high Cs in bars 5 and 9.
  • Invent some actions for each verse to help them remember the different words, but don’t make them too complicated, or they may forget to sing!

resources.title: Minibeast Percussion Pulsework
resources.content:
[{"key":"55f2e6e8b203cb9f","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"
  • To begin to internalize pitch and pulse
  • To begin to recognize a range of timbres
  • To explore how different timbres can be used to create sound effects and imagery
","title":"What’s achievable","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/green-star-1614702483w2iKm.png"}},{"key":"5a1ed30598ee65df","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Amplified sound system; backing track for this song; pitched and unpitched percussion instruments

","title":"What you need","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/blue-wrench-16147025258WedI.png"}},{"key":"75da5e085c4d76d2","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

This song has a strong four-beats-in-a-bar pulse. Talk about what a pulse is (like a heartbeat or a ticking clock). To help the class to ‘feel’ the pulse, see if they can march on the spot or around the classroom in time to the music. Can they now ‘creep and crawl’, still keeping to the beat?

Try adding some simple unpitched percussion, e.g. guiros and woodblocks, to emphasize the pulse. They could play on all four beats of the bar, or as a challenge, just beats two and four, e.g. sh tap sh tap.

What is the song about? Listen carefully to the words. Is there a story? Listen carefully to the backing track and see if you can pick out the different instruments and sounds that might relate to this – which sounds represent the caterpillar, and which the butterfly? Think about other sounds that you might hear in a garden, e.g. the wind in the trees, bees buzzing, birds singing etc. How might you reflect those sounds with instruments from your classroom instrument box?

","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}},{"key":"f0ed394da694084e","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Try varying the dynamics to create contrast between the different verses of the song. Play ‘guess the dynamic’ with one group of children performing either very softly (pp), softly (p), moderately loudly (F) and very loudly (f) – without shouting or straining their voices!). Can the other group guess the dynamic?

","title":"Step It Up!","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/u1873-1614695091mFFrP.png"}}]
resources.summary: Learn about beat and pulse as you march, creep and crawl in time to the music. Then, use listening skills to identify how certain musical timbres can create sound effects and imagery, creating musical stories.

resources.title: Caterpillar Rhyme
resources.content:
[{"key":"e1dcfc938c55084c","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Can the children spot all the rhyming words in this song? For example: 

  • Munch, lunch
  • Crawl, wall
  • Feast, beast

How about the alliteration? 

  • Cabbage, kale
  • Creep, crawl
  • Chewing, chomping
  • Lettuce leaves

Can they come up ideas of their own? Perhaps writing a poem or some expanded noun phrases to describe another minbeast of their choice. These would look great on a classroom display alongside some minibeast artwork. 

","title":"","noMargin":false}}]

resources.content:

The songs Caterpillar Munch<\/em> and Tadpole Song<\/em> provide great opportunities to investigate the life cycles of frogs and butterflies<\/strong>. Can the children do their own research into one of these creatures, using books and\/or computers? Discuss various ways they might like to present their results such as using PowerPoint, as a presentation to the class or in poster format.<\/p>\n","title":"","noMargin":false}}]
